comments.text:
I live in Denmark, and I think it’s pretty great. I have two chronic conditions (type 1 diabetes and chronic migraines) and don’t have to worry about treatments or payments for the treatment.

I’m currently a student and pay no tuition and get paid around $1000/month before taxes as a stipend because I’m studying. I have a part-time job cleaning a few offices and make the equivalent of $26.71/hour.

Yes, taxes are high, but they aren’t that high either. When my education is done, my expected wage as a new employee is around $7360/month before taxes and the unemployment rate is 1%. The effective income tax rate for that wage is 34.5%, and it covers almost everything you can and can’t imagine. This isn’t just for “free” healthcare and tuition free education; it covers subsidized childcare, rent aid for low income earners, pensions, unemployment payments, disability aid and payments, maintenance and building of new infrastructure and on and on.

After 10 years of experience I can expect a wage of $10,400/month and the effective tax rate for that will be 37.3%. This is of course if wages don’t rise in that time, which they certainly will.
